They didn't make it through, but let's put it in perspective. This isn't a case of CGI kids this is real life.
Breaking down the Knight Capita
What Knight markets prices down to. It is most important to understand that Knight sells "makers" and "takers." Here's how it works: The maker is the institution that places a bid and the taker is the institution that takes the bid. When the maker offers at $5.14 and the taker is ready to sell at that price, Knight averages the two deals to result in $5.15. It comes out of Knight's assets. And that is the difference between a maker and a taker. Makes are the supply-side of the market. Knight takes their orders and lists them on public platforms; however, if the prices are either excessively high or low, the orders are rejected. So it is just rejected is what it is. And contrary to what I have read three or four... one really good... Jason Trenn wrote a good article but clearly misunderstood how this entire system functions, distinguishing between the bid-side and the offer-side where Knight acts as the maker by supplying bids. The buy side then sets the quoted prices, meaning Knight always pays based on these quotes. Essentially, the best bid-or-offer (BBO) from consolidated feeds becomes our trade reference—essentially trading across multiple competing markets. It is simple.
David Kabiller doesn't care if you believe it. He won't use a word to describe what Knight bought and sold. As he wrings his hands, his mouth nearly springs open to utter more words, infused with each point by an influx of vigor and sincerity. Yet, Kabiller, the avatar of Knight Industries, enjoys his computers and relishes discussing them — and he does not find other people's opinions on them particularly compelling.
